speakerposition: topic
maintopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT AMENDMENT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution.
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Bankruptcy Act, and to provide for the administration of the act by the Minister of Finance, and for the appointment of a superintendent of bankruptcy and the payment of his expenses from a percentage of the gross receipts out of the sale of any property of the debtor; and to provide for such assistants as may be required, and for the licensing of trustees and payment of fees therefor.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The Bankruptcy Act, as it appears on the statute books of Canada today, was originally passed in this house in the session of 1921, and we have now had ten or eleven years' experience of the operation of that legislation. As the years have passed, many suggestions have been made in regard to amendments to the act in very many respects, and from time to time certain amendments have been made with the idea of improving the machinery which is available under the Bankruptcy Act in respect to the estates of insolvent persons. Recently the whole subject of our bankruptcy legislation was considered at a meeting of the Canadian Bar Association, and a committee of the members of that association, who are considered to be experts on the subject of our bankruptcy law, was appointed for the purpose of considering whether certain further amendments should not be made to render the act more workable and less expensive in its operation. I have had submitted to me a recommendation of the committee which was appointed by the Canadian Bar Association, and that association also submitted a draft bill on the subject. That report and the bill then submitted have been very fully investigated by
the law officers of the Department of Justice, and it was decided that it would be in the interests of the whole community if certain of the proposals contained in that report were adopted as amendments to the present Bankruptcy Act. The whole draft bill as submitted has not been adopted, but in addition to that various suggestions have come to the department from every province in Canada in regard to amendments to very many of the clauses of the present act. These suggestions have come from very responsible bodies: from wholesale dealers' associations, from retail dealers' associations, from some farmers' organizations, from chartered accountants, from lawyers, from judges, and, in fact, from almost all classes of our community. I shall have placed at the disposal of a committee which I will propose shortly a very large number of these suggestions in order that they may be fully considered, because a great many of them have not been included in the measure which has been drafted pursuant to the resolution now under discussion.
Briefly, may I state that the most important provision in connection with the present resolution is the one for the appointment of a superintendent in bankruptcy. It is by reason of that proposed amendment that the matter is now brought before the house by way of resolution. It will involve some charge on the public fund, and for that reason it has to be introduced into this parliament by means of resolution.
The proposal to appoint a superintendent in bankruptcy is a new departure. It has been considered by many associations, including the Canadian Bar Association's committee, and has been very seriously recommended. It is thought that we should have some controlling power attached to the Department of Finance, as proposed in the bill, in order that all the machinery involved in the Bankruptcy Act may come within the purview of a superintendent who will have full power to deal with the trustees who are appointed in various parts of the Dominion of Canada in regard to the winding up of insolvent estates. The chief complaint which is made against the present law is the expense attendant upon its operation. Complaints come in from time to time that in many cases there is nothing left for the creditors because of the expenses of winding up, that the fees paid to trustees, to lawyers and to inspectors eat up the whole available estate so there is nothing left for the creditors.
That is a situation, of course, which we should remedy if it is possible to do so, and
Bankruptcy Act

it has been considered that if someone had a commanding position in control of the whole machinery, having jurisdiction throughout the whole of Canada, much of the expense now involved in the winding up of estates might be done away with. I believe that proposal has been very well received in all the trading communities of Canada. This resolution mentions the appointment of a superintendent, and the bill will provide for the appointment of a superintendent with very wide powers.
It is my intention, if this resolution passes and the bill is introduced, to submit the bill to a special committee of this house-I would suggest a fairly large committee-in order that not only the proposals contained in the bill may be considered but that other proposals from responsible bodies, corporations and individuals in every part of Canada who have submitted proposed amendments, may be considered as well. I think the time has come when we should have a very full discussion of the question of amending the Bankruptcy Act, and if the bill is given second reading I will ask that it be referred to a special committee in order that these proposals may receive the fullest study and consideration and that an effective amending bill may be submitted to the house as a result. I submit the present bill more as a basis for discussion. The government is not wedded to all the proposals it contains, though we have gone over the bill very carefully and we think the proposals contained in it will considerably improve the present measure. It may be, however, that there are other amendments just as necessary as those we have suggested in the bill, and we will welcome those suggestions from any quarter whatever.

speechtext:
Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, there is a matter I should like to bring to your attention. I have been handed a copy of the Montreal Daily Star of March 1, in which there is an editorial headed "Bennett, the Vancouver Sun, and Money." In part the editorial states:
Mr. Coote, Progressive member for Macleod, deserves the thanks of the people of Canada for introducing his resolution calling for an inquiry into Canadian money because it elicited from the Prime Minister, not only a dear exposition of the character of money, but a very definite and emphatic assurance that his government proposes to keep Canadian money firmly founded on a gold basis.
In other respects Mr. Coote is not so much entitled to gratitude; for, while Mr. Bennett's analysis of the existing situation steadies public confidence in our money, Mr. Coote's figures and surmises tend to unsettle it.
This is not because Mr. Coote is right and Mr. Bennett wrong. It is wholly because money is a mysterious thing to most people, and they do not know for certain that rash figures flung out by glib theorists as well as visionary theories flung out by glib figures may be most misleading in their deductions.
I think the inference is that I have been quoting rash figures, but I want now to challenge the Star to show where my figures were wrong. Rash figures were flung out glibly enough in this debate, but not by me; they were used by the Prime Minister. Some of his figures were so far from the facts as to make one wonder whether he was really serious or knew what he was talking about on that occasion.

On the occasion of which I speak the Prime Minister was discussing the causes which led to the abandonment of the gold standard by Great Britain. I should like to refer to the remarks which he made then and, if I may, I shall be glad to quote his figures. He
stated that the great excess of imports over exports by Great Britain was responsible for forcing the old country off the gold standard, and he gave the figures. On page 647 of Hansard he is reported as saying:

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will speak very candidly. A man like tihe Minister of Labour, who gave us such an exhibition of humbug last week-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-could not answer a
pertinent question about white-collared unemployed asked by a member of parliament. I do not wish to lodge any personal attack against any 'hon. member in this house, but when I address a question to a minister, however big 'he might be, I think 'he should answer decently.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is pretty hard to redress an old tree, but I will try out his education. I have succeeded in connection with some hon. members, and I will begin on him. People suffering in this country had hoped for unemployment relief from this man but he is good only for making bold replies to hon. members and showing his gross ignorance in the House of Commons of Canada. It is time to put a stop to that, and I think the Prime Minister should tell his colleague to go away, to leave the cabinet, so that he may be replaced by a decent man who knows something about the troubles of the people. He should be replaced by a working man, and not by one who sneers at the troubles and miseries of the unemployed. He should be replaced by a man who understands the sufferings of others, and who is ready to come to their rescue in a decent way, a man who uses decent language and has decent thoughts. Decent thoughts are expressed by decent language, but we cannot expect decent
language from a minister who answered so boldly my hon. friends from Shelburne-Yar-mouth (Mr. Ralston) and Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiseit) and other hon. members on this side of the house who have tried to obtain from him an answer which might at least to some degree be intelligent. We are here, Mr. Chairman, to exercise our rights and privileges as members of parliament, and I do not mind what the dumb minister may say to me. He can tell me' that Jean Francois Pouliot is a crazy fellow, that he is too curious, but he cannot say that the member for Temiscouata county, in the province of Quebec

a county composed of fifty thousand souls and over twenty thousand electors-is not entitled to receive a courteous answer from any one on the treasury benches. If the minister's manners can be tolerated in the mining districts, if the miners there are to be treated discourteously by men of his calibre, I protest at any attempt to treat members of parliament in the same way. I say once for all-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should like those members who are jeering at me to be just as independent as I am to speak their will freely instead of making such silly jokes when a man is upholding his own views, and also the views of the Canadian electorate, the views of those who are weak, the views of those who are in distress, because they are not properly taken care of. I have been sent here to exercise my rights and privileges as a member of parliament. I am afraid of no man. If the minister was as thin as a consumptive I would have some regard for him, but he is a big, stout, strong fellow, and I like to fight such men. If he were as big and solid as the rock of Gibraltar-and he has some of the characteristics of rock when he treats the troubles of the unemployed so unsympathetically-if his heart is as hard as the rock of Gibraltar, I warn him-and my words are definite and final-we will teach him manners, so that when he goes into the far north the miners will say: "Oh, well, he is a gentleman! What did you do to him, did you give him a shave, a hair-cut, a massage-7"

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
"-He has been polished
by His Majesty's loyal opposition in the House of Commons." That is all I have to say for the present, Mr. Chairman.

Supply-Mines Branch
Mines branch, for investigation of mineral resources and deposits; of the mining and metallurgical industries, and of mineral technology; wages, expenses of testing and research laboratories, investigations by Dominion Fuel Board, including salaries and all other expenses, $238,500.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the minister give us a brief outline of the changes in staff that bring about the reduction?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Mines):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The reduction is made up partly of the ten per cent reduction and partly of the lesser amount being purchased in the way of supplies and things of that character which we think we can get along without during this year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are there any men who are not on the permanent staff but are on t'hc prevailing rate of wages who are covered by this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, there are some.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When the Minister of Finance was discussing his resolution some time ago it was pointed out to him that there were some prevailing rate men on the canals who had already had a reduction in wages, and I gathered from him that when his bill was in committee he might take those men into consideration. I am wondering what effect it will have if some of these men whom we are now dealing with in this item have already had a reduction in wages, and if it is proposed now that they shall suffer a further ten per cent reduction.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There has been no reduction prior to this; this is the only one.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is any assistance being provided for gold mining under this particular vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is no direct monetary assistance but there is the usual assistance by way of investigation which is carried on in the mines laboratory.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is a reduction in this vote of $61,500, which is rather a respectable amount. Is it intended to reduce the staff there as well? Then ten per cent mentioned by the minister would not account for this $61,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There are altogether about ninety employees, fifty being on prevailing rates, and the reduction in salaries there, together with the saving made in the purchase of supplies, accounts entirely for the total reduction.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is no intention to reduce the activities of the Fuel Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do any of these men who are on prevailing rates earn less than $1,200 a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This applies in its entirety to the labourers whose rate of pay was 50 cents an hour, less ten per cent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If there are any men on prevailing rates who are earning less than $1,200 a year-and I assume there are-then unless t'he five per cent reduction which is to apply to the permanent service applies to them also it will not be in keeping with what apparently the minister has in mind at present. In other words, the permanent civil servants earning less than $1,200 are now being reduced, practically speaking, by five per cent instead of ten per -cent, whereas, the -men on prevailing rates who are probably earning much less than $1,200 will be getting a ten per cent cut. I was wondering whether the minister would consider this point. These men ought not to be given the full ten per cent reduction but should be reduced in line with those earning less than $1,200 in the permanent service.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I shall be glad to look into the matter when the act is -being applied, although the hon. gentleman will note that the prevailing rate has been established at 50 cents an hour, which probably is more than the actually -prevailing rate. I am not complaining about that, however. I shall look into the question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At first glance this would appear to be a neglect of the great mining industry,, because there is a reduction of $61,500 for investigation of mineral resources, deposits, and so on, and other kindred activities. I should like the minister to tell us whether this is the purpose, or whether we have been spending too much in previous years. Will he promise to give this matter further attention and provide some further encouragement later on? It seems to me a poor policy indeed to neglect this great mining industry which every year has grown to greater and greater proportions.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have been personally
interested in the Mines department for many years, and any curtailment of the activities of that branch would receive my very reluctant consent. But in this connection I do not think
Supply-Mines Branch

we need fear that the activities of the department will be interfered with in any way. The natural resources have been all turned over to the provinces, and of necessity that transfer included some of the activities formerly carried on in the Mines department. I have gone into the question of the operation of the department with the heads of the various branches, and I can assure the hon. member that the mining industry will not suffer by reason of what at first glance would seem to be a substantial reduction.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What branch of the mining industry is under the control of the federal department? If we have no control in the provinces where is our activity carried on?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The federal department
of mines at no time exercised control over the mining industry in the various provinces, but for many years, either through the Geological Survey, or, by itself, the department has exercised a sort of jurisdiction over mining in general, by way of advice and research, either alone or in cooperation with those provinces having mining departments of their own. The mines branch is the only place in Canada where research work, such as they carry on, can be accomplished; none of the provinces have the equipment or men trained and equipped to carry on these investigations. For instance, any mine in any province having a problem can request the assistance of the mines branch and can obtain the benefit of their experience and advice in dealing with a metallurgical or other problem.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where is this research work carried on, here in Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Could the minister say
what results have been obtained from the tests which have been made with regard to the coal deposits in northern Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Investigations have been
carried on in connection with the northern Ontario lignite field. These investigations and tests are still proceeding, and I am advised that there has been no certain conclusion drawn as to the possible commercial value of these deposits, or as to whether they may serve any certain locality in the near vicinity. I presume that information will come only when the tests have been completed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I presume
the laboratories are not as busy as they were formerly, but I should like to ask the min-

ister if he thinks he will have sufficient funds to meet all the demands for investigations and tests in connection with minerals generally, now that he has very well equipped laboratories for the purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know the hon. member,
who was formerly Minister of Mines, takes a deep interest in this subject, and I can assure him that the vote will take care of any investigations that may be reasonably expected. One reason why the vote remains about the same, or is slightly reduced, while the laboratories are capable of taking care of the greater activity of the mining industry, is the excellence of the laboratories themselves, which were started some years ago and which were brought up-to-date quite recently. I can assure the hon. member that the laboratories are probably as good as will be found on this continent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would the minister be kind
enough to advise the committee whether any investigations were made by the fuel board during the past year, or whether any are in contemplation for the coming year, in connection with extending the experiments which were made in order to demonstrate the economic possibilities of pulverized coal? I recall that the late government installed a pulverized coal unit in the furnaces which heat this building. Last spring I inspected that unit, and from my conversation with the employees I gathered that it had been very successful both in reducing the amount of fuel used and in the saving of money. There was a good opportunity for comparison because some of the units used ordinary coal which was shovelled in by hand.
The third point on which I would like information is this: Having gone to considerable expense to demonstrate the usefulness of that system, the minister might give it more publicity by publishing a pamphlet which would be available to the trade generally, because after all, while a good purpose was served by demonstrating the commercial possibilities of this system, it must be given publicity in order to encourage people to install these pulverized coal units, which will help to provide a market for our coal.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At the request of the
British Columbia government quite elaborate tests were made in connection with pulverized fuel, and a report was prepared and forwarded to the British Columbia government. I have looked over the report but I frankly confess that it is so highly technical that I was unable to follow it beyond the narrative descriptions it contained. The results were not

Supply-Mines Branch
altogether disappointing, but they were not as hopeful as they might have been with respect to the coal sent here for test. I assume that the British Columbia government will publish the report if they believe the tests show that the use of that sort of coal is practicable. I do not believe the department has under consideration, and certainly the officials have not discussed the matter with me, the publication of the report here.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That was not quite what I
had in mind. I am aware of that exceedingly technical report which I think no one but a highly trained engineer could understand. That report was sent to the British Columbia government, and I understand they forwarded it to the various mine owners who had furnished the coal, so that if they wished they could make use of the information obtained. That report had more to do with the heat units, the amount of moisture and matters of that kind. What I had in mind was the demonstration which the department put into effect in the plant by which these buildings are heated, where they installed a pulverized coal unit whereby the fuel is pulverized and fed to the boiler in the usual pulverized coal method which I think is called the screw method. The results were highly satisfactory. While I obtained them personally, so to speak, I was not able to give them that publicity which I think they deserve. It was a practical demonstration, which was very important to people interested and which should have been made public throughout Canada, that it was highly successful to use pulverized coal in a heating unit of that description. If the minister would authorize the preparation of a brief pamphlet giving information such as I obtained from that demonstration, it would not cost very much; it would be very interesting; no doubt the press would publish it and it would be of great benefit to the coal industry as a whole. That is what I had in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines

made here for the Department of Public Works.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Vancouver assay office, in case some hon. members are not familiar with its history, was established some years ago, in fact after the opening up of the Yukon, for the purpose of being able to purchase at Vancouver, Yukon and coast gold, thereby keeping the gold in Vancouver instead of having it shipped to Seattle. Beginning late last year, I think, the larger depositors, the mines up on the coast like the Pioneer and the Premier, found it more convenient to ship their gold to the Mint. I am not just sure by what method these shipments would be made, but they would be either by registered mail or more probably by express. At any rate, I inquired as to the reason for the falling off in the work of the assay office. There was no necessity for making four assay tests of shipments and in this way the expense was greatly reduced because each assay is expensive. That accounts in the main for the difference in cost.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: This is, after all, a species of advertising. The mines branch of the federal government is engaged chiefly in research and in mapping the results of the geological parties that go out. maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It strikes me that the reduction mentioned by the minister is not encouraging to the miners; it would seem that the government is anticipating less business in the coming year than there was in the last. True, the minister has said the fuel board has come to the conclusion that a smaller quantity of coal will be moved in the coming year. In view of that, and in view of the promises made by the Prime Minister during the election campaign of 1930 to the effect that he would bring into operation a national fuel policy which would increase the sale and the use of Canadian coal, I must say there is a very poor outlook. This year in the discussion of estimates we hear the government say that they do not anticipate as much coal will be sold during the coming year as in the last. I was wondering if the minister could tell us whether or not the government has a national fuel policy which will give some encouragement to the miners.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This item is not reduced
because the government anticipates the use of less coal during the coming year than was used in the last, but because of the experience gained from our operations last year. The

Supply-Geological Survey
movement of coal east and west from the Canadian fields into the central part of Canada is something of a very difficult and intricate nature. Anyone who has given the matter consideration-and I presume the hon. member has-is familiar with that fact. It is not because we do not anticipate using more coal next year than we did last that this item is reduced, but because of the experience gained last year after the subventions were increased. We found last year that we did not need the appropriation we anticipated we would need. I can say however that the use of Canadian coal is increasing. The western coal operators, after the adjustment had been made early in 1931, fully anticipated they would be able to displace foreign fuels in their natural market, which of course, extends as far east as Manitoba. Their anticipations were in large measure realized. But in common with all of us, they did not anticipate the falling off that took place in the consumption of coal. With the added assistance by way of subvention, if the normal consumption had taken place, the western coal operators and the miners would not be facing their present difficulties. That is the problem presently under discussion. It applies with almost equal force to Nova Scotia. The problem, I assume, confronted my predecessor as it confronts me to-day, of getting coal as far as the central zone in order that nobody shall bear a greater burden than he should be called upon to bear with respect to the marketing of our coal. The whole subject is again under review in the light of present conditions, and I hope we shall be able to find a solution to enable our coal mines to carry on until the consumption of coal becomes normal again.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is one large item estimated, but the other figures are accurate.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In view of the fact that there is a strike in progress in the Alberta coal fields, may I ask if the minister is making any effort to bring the conflicting parties together?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Just so soon as I heard of the impending labour trouble in some of the mines of southern Alberta and the Crowsnest pas I got in touch with the premier of Alberta and asked him to keep me advised as to what was going on. I assured him that the services of the federal Labour department were at his disposal, and that we would gladly cooperate with him to have the dispute amicably adjusted. A number of communications have passed between the premier of Alberta and myself, and as late as yesterday I wired him with respect to a suggestion that he had made a week or ten days ago for the appointment of a commission to study the coal industry generally in his province. With that suggestion I have no quarrel; his judgment may be the best in that regard. I can assure the hon. member that I am keeping in close touch with the situation, and that the department is quite willing and ready to offer its services in order to bring about an amicable arrangement.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister told us that $628,000 was paid on account of this subvention. How many tons of coal was that paid on?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have not added up the figures, and I trust I shall not be held too strictly to account if they are not absolutely
171S

accurate. These are the figures for the nine months to t'he end of 1931: Alberta to Ontario 22,634 tons; Alberta and British Columbia- that is Crowsnest .pass-to Manitoba and western Ontario, 180,248 tons; Saskatchewan to Manitoba and western Ontario, 60,221 tons; British Columbia, export and bunker coal, 53,561 tons; Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to Quebec and Ontario by rail and water, 332,159 tons; all rail-this is an estimate-
95,000	tons. If I might revert to the question asked by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) the estimated item was $140,000. Those figures will give the amount of coal moved under the subvention.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That makes less than
1,000,000 tons, and a portion of that coal would be moved anyway. How much of it is new business to Canadian mines?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not those figures before me, but as regards the territory served I think I should be safe in saying that all coal moved into western Ontario would be new business for the mines.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That would be 180,000 tons.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I know that in the Manitoba market the western mines have captured the major portion of the trade. I do not want to be extravagant in my figures, but I should say they have now eighty per cent of that market.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the
subsidy was increased it was estimated that the mountain mines in British Columbia and Alberta would supply 200,000 tons which came in from the United States to the Winnipeg market and as far west as Portage. I do not know whether that hope has been realized. I am referring to bituminous coal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What I wish to find out is what this policy is costing us. As nearly as I can gather from the minister's statement, we have displaced a quarter of a million tons }f American coal at a cost of two-thirds of i million dollars. That involves the loss of a jertain amount of revenue which was derived from the coal that came in from the United States. How much is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not the figures.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are several things which it is necessary for us to know before we can arrive at a conclusion, and I suggest that the item be allowed to stand until the minister can tell us how much we have paid out in subventions, how much new business has been brought to Canadian mines, how many men 
have been employed, what wages they have received, what revenue we have lost through the non-importation of American coal, together with all other factors that might help to throw some light on the question. We want to know definitely what the policy is costing us.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What rates of subvention are used in estimating the amount that will be necessary for next year? I have endeavoured to look up the rates but I have not had an opportunity to verify them. As I recollect however, last year there was a two dollar maximum on all coal railed from Nova Scotia to Montreal. There was a two dollar maximum contribution to Montreal, and the forwarding rate into Quebec points was one-fifth of a cent per ton mile with a maximum of seventy-five cents, and a one-third cent ton mile with a maximum of $1.50 into Ontario. Is there any increase in these rates of subvention included in the amount for which the minister is now asking the committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No; these estimates are based on the subventions as indicated by the hon. member.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The plight in which the
miners of Nova Scotia at present find themselves, through various contributing causes and factors, with which I have no doubt the hon. member is conversant, was brought to the attention of the government by the premier of that province. The seriousness of the situation would impress itself upon anybody, and the matter was immediately taken into consideration. The railways and large consumers of American coal were interviewed, and others were interviewed without delay in an endeavour to find additional markets for Nova Scotia coal in order to relieve the situation of the miners there. I think I can safely say to the hon. member that the negotiations will very shortly, in fact I hope within the course of a very few days, come to a successful conclusion. The matter is under the careful consideration of the government, who are acting in harmony with the railroads and keeping in touch with those interested in Nova Scotia, and we hope that these newspaper reports will be fully justified in fact. That is my hope, and I believe that the hon. member will join with me in that hope.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I can assure the hon.
gentleman that I most heartily join him in that hope, but I want facts on which to base the hope. I understand my hon. friend to say that so far as subventions are concerned there is no increase proposed in the vote here which would justify the hope that any more coal will be moved under these subventions. Is that so or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is quite true; this
vote does not take care of extra subventions
If, however, arrangements can be made to find a market for the coal, and if the government feels that it is wise and desirable to see that the coal is moved into the consuming market-and I think my hon. friend will agree with me that the government will do everything in its power to have this done -then ways and means can be found to bring about that end.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The market is there. The railways will use the coal; there is no doubt about that: the railways will be a market for the coal. The question is to get sufficient subvention to induce the railways to take it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How much subvention
would the hon. gentleman suggest would be necessary for the railways to use an extra million tons of coal?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should think my hon.
friend would know that better than I would; he has the benefit of the assistance of the fuel board, which is doing the figuring. I say the railways provide a very substantial market; I know they will not use one million tons, but apparently my hon. friend has adopted that figure. Then I ask him what markets he proposes to utilize in order to reach that figure, because I want to impress upon him that it is no use to provide for one million tons on the one hand and take away half a million tons on the other because of the falling off in consumption. The Nova Scotia coal fields need to sell a million tons more, and that cannot be done if on one hand you provide for a million tons and, on the other, you have to meet a falling off in consumption.
I want to ask my hon. friend, who says that the government is exploring the matter now, what markets he expects to find for a million tons of Nova Scotia coal.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Every effort is being made to find markets for a million tons or more of Nova Scotia coal. I trust my hon. friend will not blame this government if the consumption of coal falls off; that is something we cannot control, but we do recognize that it is desirable to find a market for that much Nova Scotia coal. That effort is being made by the government, and I hope it will be successful very shortly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the subvention now extend to railway coal?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think railway coal is all moved on the o.c.s. rate.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The subvention has not heretofore applied to the movement of railway coal?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No.
Supply-Geological Survey

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should
like to ask the minister a question with regard to the subvention on lignite coal from Saskatchewan destined for the Manitoba market. Last year the original rate of fifty cents per ton was changed to a mileage rate of one-seventh cent per mile. That, we felt, rather worked against the coal of that area reaching the Manitoba market, because the difference amounted to ten cents a ton. I think possibly that had a little to do with the trouble in the Estevan coal fields last September. I pointed out the unfairness of this change on two or three occasions last year, and I should like to know if the minister has any intention of giving that coal area a little better treatment by way of subvention than was given last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am told that mines such as the Truax-Traer can compete in the Manitoba market against coal from Alberta and the Crowsnest. However, I will go into the matter again, and if we are able to discover a discrepancy that will be taken into consideration.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister seems to gauge the activities of that coal field by the activities of the Truax-Traer mine. That is only one company, though it is a large one. They do surface mining, a stripping process, which is not really coal mining as we know it. Most of the mines do deep seam mining, and of course that is a little more expensive. We do feel that something of an injustice was done that area last year by reducing the subvention ten cents a ton, which gave the Alberta fields that much of a preference in the Manitoba market. I hope the minister will take this into his serious consideration and see if we cannot have the subvention restored to where it was before last year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I had intended to ask one or two questions somewhat along the lines asked by the hon. member for Weyburn, but I understand that the item is to stand so that this information may be brought down, so I will let my questions stand also. I hope the minister will realize that the matter is very important, because after all this item embodies the fuel policy of the government, which is a matter of very great interest to everyone, particularly to those who represent coal areas. We desire to find out not only the coal policy itself but also the increased business that has been brought about by the application of this policy. We realize that coal consumption may fall off, so that perhaps it is not an absolutely fair criterion of the success 
of the policy, but surely it would be fair to judge it by the increased percentage of business handled by Canadian mines in preference to mines in other countries. Keeping that in mind, I hope the minister will bring down all the information necessary to enable us to find out very definitely just how successful the policy has been, what increased business has been brought about by it, and what has been the cost to the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I shall be very glad to get that information and bring it down, and to let this item stand in the meantime. Of course I am not unmindful of the importance of having the cost of these coal movements made clear; it is an important and intricate subject, on which I should like to have a full, free and frank discussion in order to have the benefit of the views of all hon. members.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I know the minister appreciates what my hon. friend just said, that this is a most important matter in the east and the west, and I am sure the minister will welcome anything which will afford the slightest possibility of the solution of a problem which has proved extremely vexing for quite a long time. The policy of subventions was inaugurated three or four years ago, and I should like to ask my hon. friend if his department has explored the market which could be opened to Nova Scotia coal if a subvention were granted which would be sufficient to justify the Canadian Pacific Railway using Nova Scotia coal as far west as Belleville, let us say, and the Canadian National Railways using it as far west as Prescott. I understand that is within what my hon. friend calls the central fuel area, which is called by other people the acute fuel area.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend means the amount of coal that would be used if Canadian coal entirely displaced United States coal on the railways? That has been investigated with respect to both railways as far west as Trenton, Prescott, Belleville, Brockville and other towns; in fact, the Dominion Fuel Board has investigated the differentials in laid down costs as far as North Bay and Cochrane. They have considered this question just as far as there was any possible hope of projecting the use of Nova Scotia coal westward, with a view to collecting all the information possible as to where the breaking point would come, beyond which no government could go in making up the differential in the laid down costs. I am sure anyone who has given study to this matter will conclude that there is" a point beyond which the difference in cost is so great as to preclude the use of eastern c.oal. That applies to both western and eastern coal, but that information is at present under

Supply-Geological Survey
review by the Dominion Fuel Board, and of course what their investigations will disclose will determine 'how much this government may have to pay as between the laid down costs in order that a million tons more or less may be given in new business to the Nova Scotia mines. I am hopeful that it will be a million tons and probably more.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend cannot
tell us the amount just on those two items for railways alone?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to be able
to satisfy the hon. member in that regard, but I have not the figures before me. They are very intricate and I did not come prepared with that information.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
While that point is
under consideration, and in order to suggest another line which the minister might have in mind when this item again comes before the committee, it may be remembered that when last year we were discussing another matter, that of unemployment relief, I brought up the same question in connection with the Brazeau collieries in Alberta, whose sole market is the Canadian National Railways. We realized then that no financial assistance is given in respect to coal used by the railways themselves, and in this particular area and others of a similar type the railways are the sole market. On that occasion I made the suggestion that if we were spending money for the relief of unemployment, there was probably no other way in which we would furnish a greater amount of employment for as small an expenditure than by paying, within a reasonable area, the difference to the railways between the cost of using Canadian coal and that of using United States coal. That has not been tried out, so far as I understand, and I know in my own area-and I will discuss this question further when the item comes up again-the issue is a live one, because the coal contracts are small and a great number of men are out of work. Therefore, as regards coal from the Brazeau and other collieries in Alberta and eastern Canada where the different mines have for their market railway lines exclusively or partially, but particularly such railways as favour steam coal alone, where the railway itself is the sole market and where at the present time coal from the United States is largely used, I hope the minister will keep in mind the question of the possibility of paying the difference in cost between the two classes of coal, Canadian and United States, to those railways in order to increase the area within which Canadian coal is used, thus supplying work to our own mines.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has the minister had any computation made as to the approximate amount it would cost to provide a market for another million tons of coal in the area that he has in mind as being possibly feasible?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not a computation that
I would care to disclose, because my research into the matter has not gone far enough for me to make any pronouncement. I think it would not be wise at the moment for me to make one, because I might have to change my viewpoint, and to give out a statement of that kind at the present time, when the matter is under consideration, might lead only to false hopes on the one hand or agreeable hopes on the other. I prefer to have the matter stand until the situation has been further investigated, and as I said a few moments ago, I hope a conclusion that will in a large measure go towards correcting the acute situation in Nova Scotia will be reached.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to join with the hon. member for Red Deer in pressing upon the attention of the minister the necessity, if the railways are to be included, of considering the movement in western Canada. If this is to be considered, it is a new departure. In the past we have been able to persuade the railways to use western coal further east on their lines than was economical from their standpoint. They could have purchased coal cheaper for the use of trains running out of Winnipeg and yet they used our western coal as far east as Minaki and Kenora. If a subvention is to be applied to the movement of eastern coal for railway use, my hon. friend will of necessity have to take into consideration tihe movement of western coal. I just want to warn him that from my past experience he is stepping into a pretty expensive undertaking if he attempts to move coal for railway uses. I am frank in saying that so far I do not believe we can justify, from the standpoint of the amount of new coal that has been consumed in the Canadian market, the expenditure in which we have been engaged for some years past in using our own coal for domestic purposes. I always felt and still feel it was a gesture in the right direction to encourage the use of Canadian coal in fields which it might not reach under existing rate schedules. But when one begins to talk about coal for railway use, one must consider seriously whether the expenditure is warranted. If, however, this is to be done by the government for the eastern movement, then of necessity the same must apply as well to the western movement.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did I understand the minister correctly when he said that the Premier of Alberta had suggested the desirability of having a commission investigate the coal industry in that province?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes. As the hon. member probably knows, some six or seven years ago there was in Alberta a commission that made an exhaustive report on the coal industry there generally. I do not know whether that report has come under his eye, but I have had occasion to look into it. That suggestion was made by the premier of Alberta, and I take it that he deemed the appointment of a commissioner would be helpful. I am not questioning his judgment in that regard.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should like to urge upon the minister the desirability of appointing such a commission; in fact, I have already advocated it in the house three or four times. In order to interest the minister in the need of a thorough investigation into the industry, I should like to point out the situation as it was brought to my attention when I was in that district shortly before coming to Ottawa. Most of the mines in the Crowsnest pass district operated about 117 or 120 days last year, so that a few men got that number of days' work. The majority of the men received only ninety to one hundred days' work.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: To what mines does the hon. member refer?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mines at Blairmore and Bellevue; and possibly Coleman is about in the same position. Some of the men got only sixty days' work. They would be mostly the day men who would receive $4.50 a day. The total wages of a man who got sixty days' work would be $270, and he must have some relief in addition to that. The man who got ninety days' work at $4.50 a day would receive only $405. Further, all those men have as the minister knows, certain deductions from their day's pay for locker fee, union fee, doctor's fee, coal and rent. Their condition is really very -bad. Some of the contract men, of course, are doing better, but even they in many cases are not making enough to keep themselves and their families, and perhaps the majority of them are family men. I am not blaming the minister for this condition, which is a difficult one, but if he had a royal commission investigate carefully the situation there, it might help the government to formulate some policy that would lead to better
"Mr. C. A. Stewart.]
conditions in that area. I hope the minister will view this proposal of the premier of Alberta in a very sympathetic manner, because I am sure that there is great need for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member that I replied to the Premier of Alberta and assured him that if he set up such a commission the department and the Dominion Fuel Board would facilitate the inquiry and give him all the data at our disposal. I do not know what is in the mind of the Premier of Alberta at the present moment, whether he intends to pursue that course or not.
Item stands.

speechtext:

surveys or land surveys? I see that they are both mentioned in this vote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There will be parties sent out by the topographical surveys branch.
That is the item we are now discussing. There may also be parties sent out by geodetif surveys.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Now that the natural
resources have been transferred to the western provinces, is this department doing any topographical work in Manitoba and Saskatchewan ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The topographical surveys branch makes surveys all over the dominion. Possibly the hon. member has reference to subdivisional surveys. That work was formerly done by this branch, but it is now a function of the provincial governments and is carried on by them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I see that vote 186 provides $142,500 for geological surveys, and it includes the wages of explorers, topographers and others. Do these overlap in any way, or are they two different branches altogether?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: These surveys do not in any degree conflict with one another. The geological survey, which the hon. member mentioned, is a function of the Department of Mines, and is carried out by that department for the purpose of discovering minerals. That is entirely different from the survey made by this branch, which concerns itself mainly with the mapping of various areas, showing the physical characteristics of the country, such as forestry, water powers and general contours.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But the maps used are just the same, are they not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certain maps are made by the Department of Mines of areas in which a special survey has been carried on. The work of that department however in no way conflicts with or overlaps the work carried on by the topographical branch of the Department of the Interior.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN CURRENCY STATEMENT OF MR. COOTE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it estimated that $20,000 will establish the reindeer quarters? Have the reindeer arrived at permanent quarters yet?

These animals are looked after by permanent wardens but I have no definite information as to the increase which has taken place. Recently a man was sent up into this territory to make a special report on the condition of the herd. A certain number of old bulls and barren cows are slaughtered each year for the relief of destitute in the Northwest Territories.
